li.a: CNN: Man who killed Minnesota lawmaker and her husband pleads guilty to murder in federal case
ABC News: Vance Boelter, suspect in Minnesota political killings, pleads guilty in federal case
NBC News: Vance Boelter sentencing, man gets two life sentences for killing Minnesota lawmaker Melissa Hortman and husband
NBC News: Vance Boelter indicted on federal murder charges in the killing of Minnesota lawmaker and her husband
MPR News: Feds say Vance Boelter acted alone in lawmaker attacks, also targeted senator's daughter
MPR News: Vance Boelter pleads not guilty in Minnesota lawmaker, Hortman shooting case
KSTP: Attorneys for Vance Boelter ask court to delay trial in state murder case

content.p: In the small hours of 14 June 2025, a man dressed as a police officer went to the homes of two Minnesota Democratic legislators in the northern suburbs of Minneapolis. At Brooklyn Park he shot Melissa Hortman, a former speaker of the state House, and her husband, Mark, both of whom died. Earlier that night, in Champlin, he had shot state Sen. John Hoffman and his wife, Yvette, who survived.

The man charged, Vance Boelter, was found after what is described as the largest manhunt in Minnesota's history. In June 2026 he pleaded guilty in federal court to all six counts against him, and a month later he was sentenced to two consecutive life terms plus 40 years. He remains accused in state court, where he has pleaded not guilty.

According to court documents summarised by NBC News and to Boelter's own account in court as reported by CNN, he went to the Hoffman home first, wearing a police-style uniform and tactical gear. When John Hoffman answered the door, Boelter said there had been a shooting and asked whether there were guns in the house. He then ordered the family to raise their hands and shot John and Yvette Hoffman. MPR News reported, citing prosecutors, that he shot the senator nine times and his wife eight. Both survived surgery, and the couple placed themselves between the gunfire and their adult daughter, Hope, Acting US Attorney Joe Thompson said. Hope Hoffman called 911.

That call led Brooklyn Park police to check on the nearby home of the Hortmans for the safety of the couple. At about 3:30 a.m., court documents say, Boelter reached their front door in a mask and wig, shouting "Police. Welfare check." Mark Hortman said he had been asleep and asked for the visitor's name and badge number. Prosecutors say Boelter then shot him and went into the house and shot Melissa Hortman as she tried to flee upstairs. The couple's dog, Gilbert, was gravely wounded and had to be euthanised. An officer who arrived fired at Boelter, who escaped, prosecutors said.

Between the two shootings, Boelter went to the homes of two other state lawmakers but did not make contact with them. Court documents said that at one house no one answered, and at the other he was spooked when a police officer approached his car.

Police found Boelter in a field near Green Isle, a mile from his home, after a search that CNN timed at 43 hours. He had left behind a notebook with a list of nearly 70 names, including politicians in Minnesota and several other states. A handwritten letter addressed to FBI Director Kash Patel was found in a car he abandoned. In it Boelter wrote that he was the "shooter at large" and claimed that Governor Tim Walz had wanted him to kill two US senators. Thompson said there was no evidence that Boelter had targeted the senators and described the letter as an apparent effort to excuse his crimes. A spokesperson for Walz did not immediately respond when NBC asked for comment.

MPR News reported in August 2025 that Boelter's motivations remained murky, and that friends described Boelter as an evangelical Christian with conservative views who had been struggling to find work, and that he sent cryptic messages from jail to The New York Times suggesting the shootings were partly rooted in the commandment to love one's neighbour. Thompson said there was "little evidence showing why he turned to political violence and extremism" and prosecutors called Hortman's killing a "political assassination". Federal prosecutors found no evidence of help from anyone else, MPR said.

A federal grand jury indicted Boelter on 15 July 2025 on six counts: two of murder through the use of a firearm, two of stalking and two firearms offences. The grand jury also issued a notice of special findings, the first step in deciding whether to seek the death penalty. He pleaded not guilty on 7 August 2025, represented by federal public defender Manny Atwal and two federal defenders from Las Vegas, one of whom leads that office's death penalty unit. Prosecutors told the court that the evidence would potentially include thousands of hours of video, tens of thousands of pages of grand jury material and data from many seized devices, and the magistrate judge designated the case complex.

On 11 June 2026 he changed his plea in a Minneapolis courtroom. Boelter pleaded guilty to all six counts, said in open court that he had planned the killings for months and had disguised himself as an officer, and admitted shooting Melissa Hortman at point-blank range. The Hoffmans sat in the courtroom. US Attorney Daniel Rosen said the offer was that if Boelter pleaded guilty and accepted consecutive life terms, prosecutors would not seek death. The Justice Department also said that a federal judge had ruled earlier in the year, in an unrelated case, that interstate stalking charges could not support a capital offence, according to ABC News. The agreement was approved by Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, a filing said. Rosen added: "Political violence is a scourge in our nation." The Hoffman family said in a statement that "there is not justice when our family and our state will never truly heal".

Judge John R. Tunheim sentenced Boelter on 23 July 2026 to two consecutive life terms and a further 40 years. He called it "the longest sentence I have imposed after hearing thousands of cases over the years, but I do believe it is deserved". Boelter told the court, "To every person I have caused loss, pain, heartache, confusion, sadness, shame or loneliness, I am truly sorry". John and Yvette Hoffman and members of both families spoke. John Hoffman said the defendant had "permanently changed my life", and the Hortmans' children, Sophie and Colin, said their parents "loved to be here on this Earth".

Hennepin County prosecutors charge Boelter with two counts of premeditated first-degree murder over the Hortman killings, four of attempted first-degree murder, one of felony animal cruelty and one of impersonating an officer. If convicted, the longest sentence he faces is life without parole. At a hearing on 2 September 2026 he pleaded not guilty and demanded a speedy trial, and two weeks later Judge Juan Hoyos set jury selection to begin on 2 November.

Less than a month after that demand, his public defenders, Raissa Carpenter and Bryan Leary, asked the judge to delay the trial because of what they called the "extensive volume of discovery", which the state has until 5 October to finish handing over. The Hoffman family said "We have waited long enough". The defence also asked the judge for a gag order to stop the Hoffmans speaking to the press; prosecutors agreed only if Boelter was also barred from posting on a Substack blog. The Hoffman family filed a personal injury lawsuit against Boelter in April 2026.
